It’s Thursday afternoon and the report has been sitting unfinished since Tuesday. Not untouched. You’ve opened it and closed it four or five times now, but can’t seem to make any progress. There’s also the dental appointment you’ve been meaning to schedule since January, and the email you finished writing last week that’s still sitting in your drafts for some unnameable reason.

You’re not procrastinating as such, because that’s a choice – like when you put off the tax return to watch the game, knowing at some level that you’re trading tomorrow’s stress for tonight’s comfort. This is about situations that run the other way. You want to start. You’ve cleared the afternoon, closed the distracting tabs on your screen, told yourself today is the day, and still nothing moves.

That strange bind, being unable to begin something you genuinely want to do, is task paralysis. I’ve spent years as a therapist working with adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), who often experience this problem because of their difficulties with executive function – the ability to plan and execute tasks. But it’s not just people with ADHD who struggle in this way. Push anyone through enough stress, too little sleep, or too far past their limits, and the same executive function system can start to falter, causing task paralysis to set in.

Goal management training

For many of my clients with ADHD, the usual support tools like task planners rarely seemed to help. When I learned about goal management training (GMT), an evidence-based programme for strengthening executive function, it stood out right away as something different. It offered a toolkit with an actual sequence of steps and specific strategies for building relevant skills. I trained in GMT, worked it into my clinical sessions, and watched it help people finally bridge the gap between knowing what they want to do and doing it.

GMT originated in the 1990s, when the psychologist Ian Robertson developed it at Cambridge University for people recovering from brain injury, whose capacity to hold a goal and act on it had been compromised. They would know that a goal mattered, hold it in mind, and yet still drift the moment something more immediate tugged at them. Robertson later refined the approach with the neuroscientist Brian Levine, and the version clinicians use today grew out of their collaboration.

Whether you have ADHD or you’re struggling for other reasons, I’ve written this Guide to show you how to use GMT to help yourself. The approach includes four stages: stop, define the goal, list the steps, check (repeated as needed). I’ll explain each of these stages in turn, then add three more that I’ve come to rely on with clients. None of the stages are complicated on their own. What makes them work is repetition: the executive functions you’re leaning on can even get stronger the more you use them.

As you read through the steps, I suggest you keep one stuck task in your mind, whether it’s that unfinished report, the unsent email, or something else, and that you try putting each step to work on it.

Pause and regulate before you act

An important part of the brain for planning and self-regulation is the prefrontal cortex. The Yale neuroscientist Amy Arnsten studies what happens to this brain region under pressure, and her findings show that even mild stress can produce measurable losses in working memory, attention, and the ability to think flexibly.

This is where GMT starts, and it asks you to do the opposite of what your instinct might be telling you. Instead of pushing harder to force your way into the task, it’s better to regulate your stress levels first. Before you plan, before you organise, before you try to concentrate, just pause. That pause provides the foundation for the remaining steps and trains you to catch the point where your attention has drifted off the task and onto autopilot. The better you get at this, the more likely you’ll be able to intervene and get back to where you meant to be.

To reset after the pause, keep it simple and physical: a few slow exhales, a walk to the window and back, a long stretch, or a roll of the shoulders. Almost everyone balks at this because they worry they won’t get back on track. Whatever you pick, give it a built-in ending. One project manager told me her breaks had a way of turning into 40 minutes, so we picked a pause that ends on its own: three exhales, counted on her fingers.

Keep your goal in mind

Imagine you head upstairs to grab your laptop and collect the laundry. On the way, your child calls out from the bathroom, you help them, and 10 minutes later you’re back at your desk without the laptop, the laundry still sitting wet in the machine. Both things were right there in your mind minutes ago. Now they’re gone.

Working memory is where you hold the information you need right now, and that includes your intentions, such as going to fetch the laptop. Unfortunately, it’s fragile and limited in what it can store.

That’s why the skill you’re training in this step is keeping your goal in mind and coming back to it, before it has a chance to decay. GMT uses the image of a mental blackboard, a place where the one thing you’re trying to do stays posted, so you can keep glancing back at it instead of trusting it to survive on its own in a crowded head.

So, on your next trip upstairs for the laptop and laundry, you keep repeating the intention: laptop, laundry. Two words, held in mind. Your child still calls out, and you stop to help, but the words are waiting when you’re done. You grab the laptop, collect the laundry, and come back down with both.

Take the next smallest step

Once the goal is in mind, you still have to take action. It’s the apparent scale of the task that often causes problems here. Shrinking the task will help. Make the first move small enough that starting costs you almost nothing.

Take the example of making that dental appointment. The first step isn’t to schedule it. Half the reason it’s sat there since January is that ‘schedule it’ is code for a whole daunting chain: find the number, check the calendar, endure the hold music, commit to a date. So, break the task into mini steps and aim to complete the very first one – give yourself permission to stop there to ensure it feels truly doable. In this example, find the number and write a note. If you get that far and you still have momentum, great – you can proceed to the next step. If not, the good thing is you’ve started the process and tomorrow you can take it further.

People rarely shrink tasks enough. A graduate student offered ‘open the document and write one sentence’ as her smallest possible move for finishing an assignment. She stayed stuck for another two weeks because the sentence was the hard part. Opening the file and reading her previous paragraph was the step that ultimately got her started. My rule of thumb now: if naming the step makes you sigh, it isn’t small enough.

Check your work against the goal

One small step is progress only if another follows it. Checking, the fourth stage in GMT, is what turns finding the dentist’s number into an appointment in the calendar. Checking means holding what you are doing up against what you said you would do, and it happens at two points.

Roughly halfway through, you ask: Am I still doing the thing I said I’d do? And, at the end of a work block: Is this the thing I meant to make? One client looked up at a check-in and found he’d spent 25 minutes reformatting the headings of a report he hadn’t started writing. He took it as proof he was hopeless. I took it as the ‘check’ doing its job. Without it, he’d have reformatted until 5 pm and called it a day’s work.

That reaction is common. People hear ‘check’ and reach for a verdict: Am I doing enough? Have I wasted the morning? Those questions stop the work cold. The useful question is smaller: Am I doing what I meant to do? It takes a second to answer, and it points you towards the task instead of back at yourself. If you’ve gone off track, reset by returning to this Guide’s first stage and restarting the cycle.

Asking is easy. Remembering to ask is the hard part, since forgetting is the whole problem. So pair the halfway check with something that happens anyway: a timer, a finished cup of coffee, the walk back from the bathroom.

Then close the loop. Every work block ends one of two ways: the task is done and you’ve achieved what you wanted, or there’s more to do – so you name the next smallest step and decide when you’ll take it. Write it where you’ll see it, or you’ll be trusting the same memory that lost the goal in the first place.

Make time visible

The four stages I’ve described so far belong together and run in order. This step and the two that follow are more like supports that you can reach for as needed.

The clinical psychologist Russell Barkley describes ADHD as a kind of ‘time blindness’, and clinicians often put it more simply: the ADHD brain lives in two time zones, ‘now’ and ‘not now’. A deadline three weeks out sits in ‘not now’, weightless and theoretical, until it lurches into ‘now’ somewhere around midnight the night before.

If that sounds like you, one antidote is to use external cues as much as possible, to move time out into the open where you can see it or hear it. For instance, an alarm labelled ‘start the report’ rather than ‘submit the report’ aims at the real sticking point, which is remembering and starting. Clients taught me to go further and name the specific action, because ‘report’ is easy to swipe away at nine in the morning, while ‘open report, read last paragraph’ is harder to argue with when you can picture yourself doing it. If you want to work for a given amount of time, set a countdown timer on your desk (or a virtual one on your screen).

Borrow structure from other people

One of the odder observations in ADHD research is that people who find it hard to get started alone often work noticeably better with someone else in the room. ‘Body doubling’ – working alongside someone else in person or over video – has spread through ADHD communities because so many people find it helps. The strange part is how little the other person has to do. No accountability, no conversation, no sense of being watched. All it takes is a shared table at the library, a co-working space, or a video call with a friend who’s heads-down on their own work.

You can use this to your advantage. Let’s say you’re struggling to write that report. Try this: twice a week, get on a video call with someone grinding through their own backlog. Say hello, name what you’re each about to start, then mute and work. You might find that just having another person on screen, head down, is enough to ease you into a task you’ve been dodging for days.

Build a ritual

If your process is working, repeat it. Sit in the same chair at the same hour with the same coffee before you work, and your brain starts to read that setup as the signal to go. The context becomes the cue. Give it a few weeks and the ritual starts to run itself: same chair, timer turned to face you, coffee on your right, the choice to begin already made before you sit down.

Keep it simple. The risk is that a ritual grows out of control, to the point where you need the right desk, the right hour, and the right playlist. Then a work trip or a sick child takes all three away and your ability to work goes with them. But one element is usually doing the real signalling, and it’s smaller than you’d think. For one of my clients it was the chair and the view out of the window. For another it was nothing but turning the timer to face her. Identify that element and you may find you can start almost anywhere.
